title: Everyone Here Came to Ask
logline: A hot sand town at the edge of a dry-zone forest where almost nobody lives and hundreds of thousands arrive, every one of them carrying something in to ask for something — and the thing they have all come to ask has no image at all: behind a painted curtain that is never drawn there is a casket whose contents the shrine will neither confirm nor deny.
human_question: When I bring something in order to get something, which part of that could anybody standing next to me actually see?

place.what_kind_of_place: A low, hot, sandy pilgrimage town on a shallow river at the inland edge of a great dry-zone national park, in a district that is otherwise scrub, paddy hollows and elephant country. It is not a place of monumental stone. The precinct is a walled rectangle of whitewashed single-storey buildings standing apart from one another under very old trees, with sand underfoot everywhere instead of paving, an avenue of offering stalls leading in, a whitewashed stupa eight hundred metres to the north, a mosque with mausolea in the same quarter, and a second, smaller shrine to the deity's consort reached across the river. The permanent population is small — a town of under twenty thousand by the last census. For a fortnight once a year it holds a crowd of a different order of magnitude, and the rest of the year it fills and empties nightly. Four traditions keep observances here; the film records that they do and ranks nothing. The principal shrine contains no image and never has: what is venerated is held in a casket behind painted curtains that are not drawn, and only the shrine's own officiants pass them.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because everything the film needs is an object, and the objects are extraordinary at night on available light. Oil in long rows of open lamps, camphor going up in white smoke off a stone, coconuts broken on a slab, garlands of red flowers, betel leaves laid in a circle of five with one in the middle, and trays of whole fruit stacked into towers under bare bulbs in the stall avenue. Sand takes light beautifully and takes footprints. The crowd is present throughout as a physical fact — a wall of moving cloth and lamplight filling a long lens, a low continuous sound of drums and voices under everything — without a single person being resolvable, which is both the ethical requirement and, as it happens, the best-looking version of the shot. And the film has an ending nobody would invent: a curtain, painted with the figure of the deity, in front of a room in which there is no figure of the deity.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The town is one of the most extreme swings in the country between empty and full. Nightly, through the year, a shrine that is shut fills and empties around the hours of worship. Annually, over about a fortnight of processions, the population goes from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands and then back to a swept avenue and closed stalls inside a couple of days. Objects move in one direction and come back changed: a tray goes in loaded and comes back with a little of itself returned; camphor goes from a white tablet to nothing in under a minute in one continuous shot; whole fruit goes in and cut fruit does not. And the leavings are measurable — the last festival's waste was weighed in four figures of tonnes. The river rises and falls and is the one thing in the film that was here before any of it.
place.when_it_looks_best: Night, and specifically the hours either side of the evening observance, when the only light in the precinct is oil, camphor, bare filament bulbs in the stalls and whatever the town's poles throw across the sand. The annual fortnight for the density; an ordinary weeknight for the emptiness, and the film needs both. First light at the river for the one cold, quiet, open frame in the film. The dry months for reliable dust and hard shadow; the sand is the ground surface and it reads completely differently wet.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A night film made almost entirely of things. Fruit stacked into towers under bulbs, betel laid in a circle, a garland threaded, camphor lit and gone, oil lamps in long rows, a tray passing across a counter into the dark and coming back lighter, sand printed and swept and printed again, a curtain, and then hard daylight on what a hundred thousand people left on the ground. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it — build, offer, wait, close, morning — and it is lit by nothing that was brought in on a truck. Nobody is introduced, nobody is followed and nobody's face is used, and the film is better for it rather than poorer: the hands, the objects and the sand carry the whole thing.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' own test, run in public, with the verdict withheld exactly where the sources withhold it. The voice reads out the one-line definition of wanting and then reads out the exemption most people who quote these books leave off — that the same act is not counted against anyone when faith, loving-kindness, compassion or a plain sense of usefulness is placed first. Then it does the honest thing and says that the test is which aim is foremost, that everybody on this sand is here on faith and almost everybody is also asking for something specific, and that nothing visible decides between those. And then it finds the one item in the list that no exemption covers — looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking — and points it at the camera and the audience rather than at anyone in frame. The film's last move is to charge itself.

sequence.on_screen: Night, ground level, long lens. The stall avenue: trays being built under bare bulbs. Betel leaves laid five in a circle with one in the middle, whole fruit stacked into a tower, a red garland coiled on top. Beside it a second bench where the fruit is being cut. Hands and forearms only; nothing above the wrist enters the frame.
sequence.voice: Two kinds of tray leave this row of stalls and they cost roughly the same. On one, the fruit is whole. On the other, the fruit is cut. The difference is not the fruit. A whole tray is carried by somebody keeping a promise they already made. A cut tray is carried by somebody making one. The sellers can tell you which is which at a glance. Nobody could tell you from the person carrying it.

sequence.on_screen: The river before sunrise. Shallow brown water over sand, black trees leaning in, a wet bank. No one in the frame. Held long, one static wide, ambient sound only.
sequence.voice: The old Sinhala compendium this film is reading opens its account of ordinary wanting with a single sentence. Wanting is the attaching that takes a thing, or a person, to be good, to be beautiful, or to be sweet. That is the whole definition. It is not an accusation, and it says nothing whatever about whether the thing is worth having.

sequence.on_screen: The avenue at full density, filmed at two hundred millimetres from a fixed position: a wall of moving cloth, lamplight and smoke, nothing in it resolvable as a person. Then the identical frame at four in the morning with the avenue empty and the bulbs still on.
sequence.voice: The same book lists the ordinary occasions when this shows up. Music. Good clothes. A good meal. A game. A trip away. Earning money, and then looking after it. And one item further down the list: giving something away in order to obtain something you want. That is the oldest plain description anybody has written of what this avenue is for, and it is written without a word of blame attached to it.

sequence.on_screen: A tray crossing a low counter into the dark of a shrine doorway, handed from one pair of hands to another. The tray goes into black. A wait. The tray comes back with part of it returned. Forearms only, both ends.
sequence.voice: Then the book does the thing almost everyone who quotes it leaves out. It says the same act is not counted against anyone when certain aims are placed first, and it names four. Faith is the first one named. Then loving-kindness. Then compassion. Then a plain practical sense of what a thing is actually for. So the question these books ask is not what was carried in. It is what was put in front.

sequence.on_screen: Extreme close, static: a tablet of camphor lit on a blackened stone and allowed to burn out in one continuous unbroken shot. Beside it, unlit and untouched for the whole take, a tray of whole fruit.
sequence.voice: And here the exemption gets genuinely hard, so let it be hard. The test is which aim is foremost. Everybody who crossed that river tonight is here on faith — nobody carries fruit through water for something they believe is not there. And most of them are also asking for one specific thing, by name. The book does not say which of those two is on top in anybody. The tray does not say. The face certainly does not say. That is not the film being careful. That is where the text stops.

sequence.on_screen: Oil lamps in a long rack, filled and lit and burning down, filmed end-on so the flames compress into one continuous line. Behind them, thrown out of focus, the crowd as moving colour and nothing else.
sequence.voice: The same books close off the easy reading of any face here. They say this kind of wanting never once arrives with displeasure. It comes either lit up or completely flat. So a bright face is not the guilty one and a tired face is not the innocent one, and a camera was never going to settle it. The whole count runs to fifty-four ordinary minds. Twelve of them are the harmful kinds. Twenty-four are called beautiful.

sequence.on_screen: The shrine front at the end of the evening. Smoke, the last lamps, and the painted curtain: the figure of the deity painted on cloth, hanging in front of a doorway. Slow push to the curtain alone, filling the frame. It does not move.
sequence.voice: There is one more item on that list of occasions, and it is the one with no exemption anywhere near it. Looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking. Every let-off the book offers is about hunger, cold, decency, kindness or use. None of them reaches that one. And behind this cloth there is no image. There never has been. What is in there is a casket, and the shrine will neither confirm nor deny what is inside it. Not one person out here has ever seen it.

sequence.on_screen: Hard cut, no dissolve, to flat mid-morning daylight: the swept and unswept ground. Trodden sand, crushed garlands, split coconut shell, bottles, a loader working a heap.
sequence.voice: Which leaves one person in this film who is certainly doing the thing the book names. A shrine that shows nothing, photographed at night because it is beautiful, for an audience that came to look. Last year fifteen hundred tonnes of what was carried in came back out as this. These books count moments of mind and not people, and in eight minutes they have not said one word about anybody here.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests do different jobs and this site needs both. C004 is the definition and the arithmetic. The Margaya defines wanting in one line — the attaching that takes things and persons to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13] — and then supplies the three facts that keep the film off every face in it: it never arrives with displeased feeling and always with the good or the middling 'taste' of its object [C004-M:L15], it is either joyful or flatly neutral [C004-M:L17], and it may arise by itself or under prompting, which may come from another person or from oneself [C004-M:L21]. The Pradeepika frames the same material as a count rather than a charge: fifty-four sense-sphere minds, thirty grouped as not beautiful and twenty-four as beautiful, of which only twelve are unwholesome [C004-P:L27], with greed described as the attaching that arises when a pleasing or a neutral object is met [C004-P:L41]. C005 supplies the occasions and, crucially, the exemptions. Its list of everyday occasions includes the exact grammar of this place — giving wealth in order to obtain pleasing objects — alongside music, clothes, food, games and the getting and guarding of money [C005-M:L5], and it says that for ordinary people most minds from waking to sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7], a claim its own digest records as the author's unquantified general statement. Then it draws the line by aim: acts done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion placed foremost are not unwholesome, and neither are acts done with discernment of usefulness foremost [C005-M:L9], food prepared or eaten for the taste is greed-rooted [C005-M:L11] while food to quiet hunger and sustain life is not unwholesome [C005-M:L13], clothing to be admired is greed-rooted [C005-M:L15] while clothing for cover and protection is not [C005-M:L17]. A place whose entire visiting population is there on faith, and is also there to ask for something specific, is where those two halves of C005 collide; and the collision is the film.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources' test is an aim and not an act, and that an aim is the one thing a camera has never been able to photograph. C004 alone would be a taxonomy read over pretty night footage. C005 alone reads as a list of forbidden pleasures, which its own digest says it is not. Together they produce the film's real finding, which is an exemption rather than an accusation. C005 names faith first among the aims that leave an ordinary act clear [C005-M:L9]; everybody at this site is there on faith; and the source nowhere rules on whether faith is still foremost in a person who has come to ask for one named thing. The film says so and stops there, because the text stops there — and because the digest's own uncertainty note records that several of these 'not unwholesome' rulings never say what kind of mind the act is instead. The pairing also hands the film the only honest place to put the charge. One item in C005's list survives every exemption the extract offers: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5]. Nothing about hunger, cold, decency, kindness or usefulness reaches it. A camera crew photographing a shrine at night because it is beautiful, for an audience watching because it is beautiful, is the clearest instance of that item in the whole film — and the shrine, which contains no image of anything, is the object of a looking that can never be completed. The move C004 makes possible is the second half of it: what is counted is a moment of mind [C004-P:L27] [C004-M:L15], so even that charge lands on an act and not on a person, including the people making the film.

concept_links.why: The Margaya's one-line definition is the spine the film reads out over the objects: wanting is the attaching that takes things and persons to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13]. The Margaya's account of the object is what makes an offering tray filmable as doctrine rather than as decoration — every object carries a good, bad or middling quality, that quality is called the object's 'taste', and a mind arising with an object arises together with a nature that relishes that taste [C004-M:L15]. A tray built so that whole fruit still has its scent when it is carried in is that sentence in physical form. Three further lines are load-bearing and are written into the sequence rather than parked in the risks: this wanting never comes with displeased feeling [C004-M:L15] and arrives either with joy or with a flat neutral feeling [C004-M:L17], which is why beat 6 refuses to read any face in the crowd in either direction; and prompting may come from another person or from oneself [C004-M:L21], which is why the film never suggests it can tell whose idea a vow was. The Pradeepika supplies the proportion that keeps the film from moralising — fifty-four sense-sphere minds, twenty-four of them called beautiful, only twelve unwholesome [C004-P:L27] — and its own definition of greed as the attaching that arises on meeting a pleasing or a neutral object [C004-P:L41]. The digest's limits travel with all of it. 'The sense world is a trap' is ruled out by the twenty-four beautiful minds. 'Follow your joy' is ruled out because joy attends greed-rooted minds as readily as good ones. The Margaya's listing of affection and love among the names of greed [C004-M:L13] is flagged in the digest as needing expert check, and this film does not go near it, which matters at a site where families come to ask about children, marriages and examinations. The claim about the first mental process after conception [C004-P:L73] is marked as a traditional doctrinal claim needing expert check and is unused. And the Pradeepika's stretch of the author's own contemporary moral commentary [C004-P:L55–L69], which includes his verdict on those who hold views of a creator god and an eternal heaven [C004-P:L65], is the single most dangerous passage in either digest for this location, because four traditions keep observances inside this precinct. It is never quoted, paraphrased, implied or answered.

C005 is where the film's question actually lives, and testing it against the source changed the film. Its list of everyday occasions contains this site's exact transaction — giving wealth in order to obtain pleasing objects — set among music, dance, scent, good clothes, tasty food, sport, and the getting, guarding and spending of money [C005-M:L5]; and it extends the same observation to courtship, spouses, the raising of children and the arranging of their marriages, concluding that for ordinary people living apart from the teaching most minds from waking to sleep are of this kind [C005-M:L7]. The digest records that last claim as the author's own general statement and notes it is not quantified, so the film states it as the book's observation and never as a measurement of a crowd. The decisive material is the exemption, and it is real: acts of getting and spending done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion placed foremost carry no unwholesome mind, and neither do they when a practical discernment of usefulness is placed foremost [C005-M:L9]. Faith is named first in that line. The source then works the same test twice more in miniature — food for the taste of it against food to quiet hunger and sustain life [C005-M:L11] [C005-M:L13], clothes to be admired against clothes for cover, cold and insects [C005-M:L15] [C005-M:L17] — and each time the outward act is identical and only the aim placed foremost differs. That is the film's structure and it is why the location is right: two trays, same price, same stall, different aim, and the difference is legible in an object rather than in a person. The film does not decide whether the exemption reaches somebody who has come to ask for one named thing, and the honest reason is in the source and its digest: the extract never rules on which aim is foremost in a petitioner, and the digest's uncertainties note that several of these 'not unwholesome' rulings [C005-M:L9] [C005-M:L13] [C005-M:L17] [C005-M:L19] do not say what kind of mind the act is instead, and that the ruling on valuable clothes worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L19] is itself notable enough to need an expert check. Four does_not_transfer lines are honoured on screen. The source does not preach minimalism or deprivation — it allows good clothes and wealth earned and spent wisely — so no frame in this film treats spending on an offering as waste. It does not say only intentions matter: it still names theft, lying and misconduct as courses of harm carried through wanting [C005-M:L3]. It does not condemn the arts, so drums, dance and lamplight are never framed as evidence of anything. And it does not license calling devoted families greedy, which at this location is the live risk, because the digest says outright that a film must not frame devoted parents that way. One line carries the film's ending: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5], which no exemption in the extract reaches, and which describes the camera and the audience before it describes anyone in frame.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That these books test an aim rather than an act, that an identical act can fall on either side of that test, and that nothing visible — not the object, not the expense, not the face — reports which side it fell on. And that the one item the books name which no exemption covers is the pleasure of looking at beautiful things, which is what a film is, so the charge the viewer has been waiting for the voice to lay on somebody else lands on the viewer instead.
what_must_be_real: The trays as they are actually built and sold, at the actual prices, at real stalls, with nothing arranged for the camera. The whole-fruit and cut-fruit distinction is filmed only if the sellers describe it that way themselves and are willing for it to be filmed; it is a reported vendors' account, not an established doctrine of the shrine, and if the sellers at the site contradict it the beat is rebuilt around what they say instead. The observance runs on its own clock and is never delayed, restarted, repeated or lit for the camera. Nothing is bought, carried or offered by the crew in order to be filmed, and no tray is followed to find out what happened to the person who bought it. The waste figure is checked against the authority that issued it before it is spoken. The crowd is filmed only at densities and distances at which nobody is identifiable; if a frame resolves a face it is cut, not blurred. Nobody is asked why they came, what they asked for, or whether it worked.
position_hint: late in the group, and preferably last: it is the film that turns the group's subject back on the people making and watching it, which only works after the earlier films have established that the books are counting moments and not persons. It also needs to come after any film that states the definition plainly, because it spends its running time on the exemption rather than on the definition. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Presenting any identifiable person as devout, desperate, credulous or acquisitive. This is the severest floor on the slate and it is structural here rather than editorial: the film is built out of objects, hands below the wrist, architecture, sand and crowd-as-texture precisely so that no frame exists that could carry the charge.

Filming any bodily austerity at all — fire-walking, hook-hanging, kavadi piercing, trance or any related observance. None of it is filmed, referenced in a shot, heard on the sound mix or implied by an edit. It appears once in the historical thread as a dating question in the scholarship and nowhere else.

Adjudicating whether petition works, in either direction. The film does not narrate the practice as superstition and does not narrate it as faith rewarded, and it carries no outcome, no testimony and no before-and-after.

Ranking, dating or contrasting the traditions that keep observances in this precinct. Their coexistence is stated; their relative antiquity is a live scholarly dispute that belongs in what_is_disputed and never on screen or in the voice.

Using the Pradeepika's own contemporary moral commentary [C004-P:L55–L69] anywhere near this location. It includes the author's verdict on people who hold views of a creator god and an eternal heaven [C004-P:L65] and his statement about their destination after death. The digest names this stretch as the author's moral argument rather than the teaching. At a site shared by four traditions, quoting, paraphrasing, implying or even rebutting it would be the worst thing this film could do.

Reading delight as guilt or flatness as innocence in a crowd. The sources say this wanting never comes with displeasure and can be bright or blank [C004-M:L15] [C004-M:L17], which is stated in beat 6 so that the footage cannot be misread.

Letting the 'most of a day' claim [C005-M:L7] sound like a measurement of the people on screen. The digest records it as the author's unquantified general statement and the voice never applies it to this crowd.

Treating spending on an offering as waste or as exploitation. The source explicitly does not preach deprivation and allows wealth earned and spent wisely, and the film's morning-after beat is about volume and disposal, not about foolishness.

Framing families as greedy. People come here to ask about children, marriages, examinations and health, and the digest states plainly that a film must not present devoted parents that way. The voice never connects the occasions list to anybody in frame.
Touching the Margaya's listing of affection and love among the names of greed [C004-M:L13], which the digest flags for expert check.

Collapsing the teaching into motive alone. The source still names theft, lying and misconduct as courses of harm carried out through wanting [C005-M:L3], and the film's aim-versus-act structure must not be heard as saying that nothing anybody does matters.
Letting the looking-at-beautiful-things inversion become a flourish the film congratulates itself on. It is stated once, flatly, in the last two beats, and it is never repeated or elaborated.

Filming inside the shrines. Photography inside active shrine buildings is reported as discouraged and in places prohibited, and the inner apartment is closed to everyone but the shrine's own officiants. The film is built to work entirely from the precinct outside the doorways, and the curtain is filmed from where any visitor stands or not at all.

Drone. A dense sacred precinct, a shrine complex, a mosque with mausolea and the boundary of a strictly protected national park. Drone is treated as prohibited throughout and no beat depends on an aerial.

Building anything on the 2024 press reporting of extortion around the offering stalls. Those are unresolved allegations about named and unnamed people at a real place. They are not the film's subject, they are not narrated, and they are recorded only as an access and safety consideration.

Repeating the site's founding story as history. The vow-before-the-battle account is the most-repeated sentence written about this place and it has no chronicle corroboration; it is handled as a story about a vow, attributed, and never as a date.
drop_if: The only way to obtain the offering-stall material is to commission a tray, stage a purchase or ask a seller to build one for the camera.
Filming at the densities the film needs cannot be done without frames in which individuals are identifiable, or without a camera position that obstructs people moving through a crowded precinct.
Permission is offered on condition that the film shows an outcome, endorses the efficacy of petition, or characterises the practice.
Any part of the access depends on filming a bodily austerity, or on being present at one.

The whole-fruit and cut-fruit distinction turns out not to be recognised by the sellers at this site, and no comparable object-level distinction exists to replace it. Without that beat the film's argument has no visible carrier and should be rebuilt elsewhere rather than asserted in narration.

connections.note: The group's two films about C005's exemptions, asked of two different things. That one asks whether the exemption covers a room built over centuries to be beautiful; this one asks whether it covers a person who has come to ask for something. Both are told to check the exemption before implying a verdict, and neither reaches one. They must not share a treatment: that film is a dim enclosed interior on available light with the camera looking up; this one is an exterior night of objects, long lenses and a hard cut to daylight.

The slate's other night film at a religious gathering, and the differentiation is deliberate at every level. That one is a straight road where hundreds of stalls give food away free and nobody asks for anything, and its signature shot is a drone pull-back to two unbroken lines of light. This one is a walled sand precinct where everything is carried in to ask for something, it has no drone at all, its widest shot is a long lens on an unresolvable crowd, and its payoff is a cut rather than a reveal.

The slate's temple festival film. That one is a daylight event of timber, rope and inertia, shot from above, whose subject is several hundred people doing one thing at one instant. This one never films the procession as an event at all: the annual fortnight is used for density and light, and the film's units are a tray, a lamp, a tablet of camphor and a curtain.

selection.reason: Rebuilt on the island's principal place of petition, where C005's exemption by aim can be tested in public against an act whose entire point is to ask for something. The location supplies a documented story that asks the concept's own question, an object that makes the aim legible where no face could, and a night film of lamps, camphor and offerings that needs no person in it.

review.note: The old film went because it was a working-site analogy, not a story: a remote valley whose cash trade is palm sap boiled into treacle, chosen because the sources' definition of wanting contains the word 'sweet'. That is a resemblance, and under the 2026-09-26 standard a great concept fit in an ordinary working location is the specific mistake the rework exists to correct; it also put a camera on a named family's dangerous unroped climb, and its final beat asked faces to carry the argument. The new location is the island's principal place of petition, and the historical binding is that the site's own charter is a vow. The story everybody tells — that a king sought the deity's protection before his war against a rival king and built the shrine in fulfilment when he won — has no corroboration in the chronicle that records the period, while the chronicle's actual notice of the place is the opposite kind of event: nobles of that town travelling to the capital for the planting of the Bodhi sapling, and a sapling planted at their town in turn. A second-century-CE inscription at the stupa names the place in stone and records a donation. The scholarly history is a rise, a collapse and a return — the cult prominent in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and major in the Kandyan kingdom, the shrine virtually abandoned through the nineteenth century after 1815 and the failed rebellion of 1817, and the mass pilgrimage of today a phenomenon of the period after 1930 — so the scale of the asking is demonstrably modern even where the site is not. And the object of all of it has no image: a casket behind painted curtains that are not drawn, whose contents the shrine will neither confirm nor deny. On the doctrine, C005's exemption was tested line by line rather than inherited: the exempting aims at C005-M:L9 are faith, loving-kindness, compassion and a practical discernment of usefulness, faith named first, and the test the source applies throughout is which aim is placed foremost, worked twice more in miniature on food and on clothing. Everyone at this site is there on faith and almost everyone is also asking for a named thing; the extract nowhere rules which is foremost in such a person, and the digest itself records that several of these rulings never say what the mind is instead. The film says exactly that and stops. The charge it does lay is the one item in the occasions list that no exemption reaches — looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking, C005-M:L5 — and it lays it on the camera and the audience, since a crew photographing a shrine at night because it is beautiful is the clearest instance of it in the film. The guards are the severest in the group and are structural rather than editorial. No individual pilgrim is a subject: the film is built from objects, hands below the wrist, architecture, sand and crowd-as-texture, so no frame exists that could hold a held face, a person followed, or anyone praying, weeping or making a vow. No bodily austerity is filmed at all, in any form, and it appears only once in the historical thread as a dating question in the scholarship. The traditions sharing the site are recorded and never ranked or dated on screen. The film does not adjudicate whether petition works and narrates it neither as superstition nor as faith rewarded. The Pradeepika's own contemporary moral commentary, and in particular its verdict on those holding views of a creator god and an eternal heaven, is named in the record as the most dangerous passage in either digest for this site and is never used, paraphrased or rebutted. Drone is treated as prohibited and no beat depends on one. Differentiation from the slate's other crowd films is written into the record: the almsgiving road is a drone film about giving where nobody asks, and the chariot is a daylight film about several hundred people acting at one instant; this is a night film of objects with no aerial and a cut for a payoff. New title from the group reassignment; both previous titles kept in aliases. Verdict reset to pending because the whole body is new.

suggested_location.region: Monaragala District, Uva Province — the dry-zone south-east, on the Menik Ganga at the inland edge of the Yala and Kumana park country, roughly 20 km by road north of the tank town at Tissamaharama and about 228 km south-east of Colombo
suggested_location.why_here: Because it is the one place in the country where the concept's question is already the site's question, and where the answer is carried by an object instead of by a person. C005 tests an act by the aim placed foremost, and here an entire town's economy runs on an act whose aim is legible in the thing bought: a tray of whole fruit is reported to be carried by somebody discharging a vow and a tray of cut fruit by somebody making one, sold side by side at the same stalls for about the same money. That gives the film the sources' distinction in physical form, filmed from the wrist down, with nobody's interior life on display. The site then supplies the two things the standard demands together. The story is documented and disputed in the most useful way: the founding account everybody repeats is itself a petition — a king's vow before a battle — and the chronicle that covers the period does not carry it, while the same chronicle does carry the place under its older name in a completely different kind of event. And the place photographs, at night, on light that is already there: oil in open racks, camphor, bare bulbs over stacked fruit, sand, whitewash, smoke, very old trees, a shallow river, and a whitewashed stupa eight hundred metres north. Finally it hands the film an ending that no invention would improve on. The principal shrine holds no image. What is venerated is a casket behind painted curtains that are not drawn, and the shrine will neither confirm nor deny what is in it — so the most looked-at object in the country is one that nobody has looked at, which is exactly the right thing to point a camera at in a film whose last move is to charge the camera.

historical_thread.story:
The most-repeated sentence about this place is a story about somebody asking for something. In the standard account — given by the shrine's own website, by the principal devotee-run archive of the site and by most of the travel and press writing — the warrior king Dutugemunu, in the second century BCE, sought the deity's protection before setting out against his rival Elara, and built the shrine here in fulfilment of that vow after he won. The site's charter, in other words, is a vow discharged: the first offering made here was a payment on a promise, and the shrine is the payment.

That account has no corroboration in the Mahavamsa, the fifth- or sixth-century Pali chronicle that narrates Dutugemunu's war at length. What the Mahavamsa does record, in the chapter on the planting of the Bodhi sapling brought from Asoka's empire in the third century BCE, is the place under an older name and in the opposite kind of event: 'the nobles of Kajaragama and the nobles of Candanagama and the Brahman Tivakka and the people too who dwelt in the island came thither also by the power of the gods, (with minds) eagerly set upon a festival of the great Bodhi-tree'; and among the saplings then distributed, one was planted 'in Kajaragama and one in Candanagama'. The earliest written notice of this place is of people travelling away from it to attend somebody else's festival, and of a tree being planted here.

The name is then attested on the ground. Two inscriptions of the second century CE were found at the stupa eight hundred metres north of the shrine; one records a donation ordered by a local ruler of the principality of Ruhuna and refers to the monument as the Mangalamahaseya of the Kajaragama raji maha vehera. The stupa itself is counted among the sixteen great places of Buddhist pilgrimage on the island, and its attribution is contested: to Mahanaga, brother of Devanampiyatissa and a regional ruler of this area in the third century BCE in the most-cited account; to a first-century-BCE build or rebuild on the inscriptional evidence in another; and, in a formula repeated on many popular pages, to a 'regional king Mahasena in the sixth century BC'.

The shrine's own documented history is later and far less tidy than the founding story. S. Pathmanathan has argued that it began as an adjunct guardian-deity shrine to Skanda-Kumara inside a Buddhist temple complex, after the thirteenth century. Heinz Bechert and Paul Younger have argued instead that the mode of veneration here preserves an indigenous Vedda pattern older than both Buddhist and Indo-Aryan influence. The first literary mention of the place as a sacred place is generally given as the fifteenth-century Tamil devotional poems of Arunagirinathar. A medieval revival is credited to Kalyanagiri Swami, a renunciate from north India of the Giri order, in the sixteenth or seventeenth century, who is said to have identified the spots of the shrines and their mythic associations.

Gananath Obeyesekere's work supplies the shape of the modern history, and it is a rise, a collapse and a return rather than an unbroken antiquity. In 'Social Change and the Deities: Rise of the Kataragama Cult in Modern Sri Lanka' (Man, 12, 1977, pp. 377–396) he argues that the cult of this deity rose to prominence in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries with south Indian immigration, became a major cult of the Kandyan kingdom where the deity served as a god of war during the conflict with the western powers, declined sharply after the British conquest of Kandy in 1815 and the failed rebellion of 1817 — the shrine, on his account, virtually abandoned for the rest of the nineteenth century — and rose again after about 1930 with the socio-economic changes of the modern period. In 'The Fire-Walkers of Kataragama: The Rise of Bhakti Religiosity in Buddhist Sri Lanka' (Journal of Asian Studies, 37:3, May 1978, pp. 457–476) he argues that the present form of the site's best-known austerity dates not from mythic times but from the Second World War.

Four traditions keep observances in the precinct today and the film ranks none of them. The Muslim presence is centred on a mosque said to have grown from the simple residence of a figure remembered as Hayathu, and on mausolea including that of Seyed Jabbar Ali Shah, recorded as having come from Bukhara in 1845; the place is identified in that tradition with al-Khidr. The Vedda connection is recorded in the deity's Vedda names and in the tradition that he married a Vedda woman, Valli, whose own shrine stands apart from the main precinct; a Vedda clan named for the temple precincts is reported as having existed in the nineteenth-century eastern province and to be now extinct. Hindu and Buddhist observance share the main shrine, whose daily and annual offerings are described by the shrine itself as following Buddhist forms.

And at the centre of all of it there is nothing to see. The principal shrine contains no image of the deity. Devotees stand before painted curtains — seven of them, in the devotee archive's account, painted with the figure of the deity flanked by his two consorts — which are not drawn apart, and only the shrine's own officiants, the kapuralas, pass behind them. What is venerated is held to be a yantra on a metal plate in a casket. In the words of the principal devotee-run archive of the site, 'It is never displayed — nor is its existence either confirmed or denied.' During the annual festival the casket goes out on an elephant, fully cloaked and unseen.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The site asks C005's question three times over, and each time it asks it about an aim rather than an act.

First, at the level of the charter. C005 draws its line by what is placed foremost: acts of getting and spending done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion foremost carry no unwholesome mind, and neither do they when a practical discernment of usefulness is foremost [C005-M:L9]. The founding story of this place is precisely a case where both aims are present and neither is separable — a king who is recorded as having asked, and won, and paid. And the historical record does the concept's own work of refusing to settle it: the vow is the part of the story that the chronicle does not carry. What the chronicle carries instead is people going somewhere else for a festival and a tree being planted. The place's own archive is silent exactly where the film would have to be silent anyway, which is why this location is right and a location with a clean documented founding would be wrong.

Second, at the level of the object. C005 makes its distinction twice in miniature, on food and on clothing: the same pot of rice, the same shirt, one aim on each side, and the outward act identical [C005-M:L11] [C005-M:L13] [C005-M:L15] [C005-M:L17]. The offering-stall avenue makes that distinction physical and sells it. Two trays, one price, one stall: whole fruit for a vow being discharged, cut fruit for a wish being made. The reason given for the whole fruit is that the scent must survive the walk — which is C004's account of an object's 'taste' and of the nature that relishes it, built into a tray [C004-M:L15]. The film can therefore photograph the sources' own distinction without photographing a mind, a face or a claim about anybody.

Third, at the level of the crowd, and this is where the film's actual finding lives. Everyone in this precinct is here on faith, and faith is the first aim C005 names as leaving an ordinary act clear [C005-M:L9]. Almost everyone here is also asking for one specific thing, and the same source's occasions list names giving something away in order to obtain a pleasing object as an occasion of greed-rooted mind [C005-M:L5]. Both descriptions fit the same person at the same moment, and the extract nowhere rules which is placed foremost in such a person; the digest's own uncertainties record that several of these 'not unwholesome' rulings never say what kind of mind the act is instead. That is not an evasion, it is the state of the text, and it is the best possible subject for a film whose whole floor is that a camera cannot show which mental factor is present. C004 supplies the guarantee that the not-knowing is doctrinal rather than squeamish: the count is of fifty-four kinds of ordinary moment, twenty-four of them called beautiful [C004-P:L27], and the wanting it does name never arrives with displeasure and is as often flat as it is bright [C004-M:L15] [C004-M:L17], so no face in the crowd could have reported the answer even if the text had given one.

And then the site hands the film the one charge the source does not exempt. C005's list includes looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5], and nothing in the extract — not hunger, not cold, not decency, not kindness, not usefulness — reaches it. The shrine at the centre of the most-looked-at place in the country contains no image; the object is a casket the shrine will neither confirm nor deny. So the completed looking is unavailable to everyone here except one party: the crew photographing the curtain at night because it is beautiful, and the audience watching for the same reason. The film ends by putting the only unexempted item in the list on itself, which is also the only place it can honestly be put.
what_is_certain: The Mahavamsa, the Pali chronicle compiled in the fifth or sixth century CE, names the place as Kajaragama in its chapter on the arrival and planting of the Bodhi sapling, in Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk: 'The nobles of Kajaragama and the nobles of Candanagama and the Brabman Tivakka and the people too who dwelt in the island came thither also by the power of the gods, (with minds) eagerly set upon a festival of the great Bodhi-tree'; and among the saplings distributed, one was planted 'in Kajaragama and one in Candanagama'. The chapter narrates events of the third century BCE.

Two inscriptions of the second century CE were found at the Kiri Vehera stupa. One records a donation ordered by a local ruler of the principality of Ruhuna and refers to the monument as the Mangalamahaseya of the Kajaragama raji maha vehera, which attests the place-name in stone.

The Kiri Vehera stands about 800 m north of the Maha Devalaya and is counted among the Solosmasthana, the sixteen great Buddhist pilgrimage places of the island. Its reported dimensions are 95 ft in height and 280 ft in circumference.

The principal shrine contains no sculptural image of the deity. Devotees stand before painted curtains which are not drawn apart, and only the shrine's officiants pass behind them; what is venerated is held to be a yantra on a metal plate kept in a casket. The principal devotee-run archive of the site states: 'It is never displayed — nor is its existence either confirmed or denied.' During the festival the casket goes out on an elephant, cloaked and unseen.

Four traditions keep observances in or adjoining the precinct: Buddhist, Hindu, Muslim and Vedda. The Muslim presence includes a mosque and mausolea, among them that of Seyed Jabbar Ali Shah, recorded as having come from Bukhara in 1845 and as having died in 1872; the place is identified in that tradition with al-Khidr. The deity's consort Valli, in Vedda-associated tradition, has a separate shrine reached across the river.

The town is in the Monaragala District of Uva Province, about 228 km south-east of Colombo, and had a permanent population reported at over 18,220 at the 2012 census. The Menik Ganga ('river of gems') runs beside it and pilgrims bathe in it before crossing to the shrines.

Gananath Obeyesekere published 'Social Change and the Deities: Rise of the Kataragama Cult in Modern Sri Lanka' in Man, volume 12 (1977), pp. 377–396, and 'The Fire-Walkers of Kataragama: The Rise of Bhakti Religiosity in Buddhist Sri Lanka' in the Journal of Asian Studies, volume 37 number 3 (May 1978), pp. 457–476. The first argues a fifteenth- and sixteenth-century rise, a major role in the Kandyan kingdom, a sharp decline after 1815 and the failed rebellion of 1817 with the shrine virtually abandoned for the rest of the nineteenth century, and a resurgence after about 1930. The second argues that the present form of the site's best-known austerity dates from the Second World War rather than from mythic times.

The 2025 Esala festival ran from a flag-hoisting on 26 June, with processions to 10 July and the water-cutting at the river on 11 July. The procession goes out from the main shrine to the consort's shrine nightly across the festival, and a widely given figure for the run of nightly processions is fifteen.

The foot pilgrimage from the northern peninsula down the east coast and inland through the Kumana and Yala parks is a documented annual practice, and recent participation has been counted by the wildlife authorities: the park warden Buddhika Vidanage is reported as giving 31,000 completing the route in 2024 and more than 10,000 entering Kumana on the first day, 20 June, in 2025.
The 2024 Esala festival at the site produced nearly 1,500 tonnes of solid waste, including four tonnes of PET bottles and 50 kg of synthetic garlands, as reported by Mongabay in July 2025.

Offering trays are built and sold at stalls at the precinct entrance and are carried in by the buyer and taken inside by the officiant, who returns part of the offering. Two independent journalistic accounts — an Explore Sri Lanka feature quoting a stallholder, and a report in The Morning quoting the shrine's Basnayake Nilame — give the same distinction: trays of whole fruit are for discharging a vow, trays of cut fruit for making a wish, with the whole fruit preferred inside because the scent survives the walk.
what_is_disputed: The founding story, and it is the single most repeated claim about the place. That Dutugemunu sought the deity's protection before the war against Elara and built the shrine here in fulfilment of the vow, around 160 BCE, is stated by the shrine's own website, by the principal devotee archive and by most press and travel writing. It has no corroboration in the Mahavamsa, which narrates that war at length. The film treats it as a story about a vow, attributed to those who tell it, and never as a date or an event.

When the shrine began. S. Pathmanathan argues it originated as an adjunct guardian-deity shrine to Skanda-Kumara inside a Buddhist temple complex after the thirteenth century. Heinz Bechert and Paul Younger argue that the mode of veneration preserves an indigenous Vedda pattern older than Buddhist and Indo-Aryan influence. A general dating of the built complex to between about 1100 and the fifteenth century is also given. These are not reconciled here and are not narrated on screen.

The first literary attestation of the place as a sacred place is generally given as Arunagirinathar's fifteenth-century Tamil devotional poems. No earlier literary designation was located in this research. An absence of earlier surviving text is not evidence about the age or standing of any tradition and the film draws nothing from it.

The dating of the Kiri Vehera. Three incompatible attributions are in circulation: to Mahanaga, brother of Devanampiyatissa, a regional ruler of the area, in the third century BCE; to a build or renovation around the first century BCE on inscriptional grounds; and, on many popular pages, to a 'regional king Mahasena in the sixth century BC'. The third is internally doubtful — the Anuradhapura king of that name reigned in the third and fourth centuries CE — and is an example of the unsourced formula that gets copied between pages. A further variant names Mahadathika Mahanaga, son of a king Tiritara, with a date of 447 CE. Nothing is averaged and no date is spoken in the film.

The etymology. Ponnambalam Arunachalam's derivation from Karttikeya Grama, the village of Kartikeya, via the Pali Kajaragama, is widely repeated and is not the only account. The film does not gloss the name.

The scale of the annual attendance. A figure of 'over 500,000 pilgrims annually' circulates on travel pages with no source attached; Wikipedia says the town's population swells to 'a few hundred thousand' during the festival. No official count was located. These are kept apart and neither is used as a number in the voice; the film uses only the counted figures — the pada yatra participation given by the wildlife authorities, and the weighed festival waste.

The length and duration of the foot pilgrimage. Reported distances include 'well over 520 km' by the older east-coast route, 'nearly four hundred kilometers', and 476 km from a named northern temple; reported durations include 45 days, 35 days and a 20-day park window, with most modern participants reported as joining for the final 90 km through the two parks. The variants are not averaged and none is spoken in the film.

The antiquity of the site's best-known bodily austerity. Believed by many devotees to descend from mythic times; argued by Obeyesekere (1978) to date in its present form from the Second World War. This is recorded here as a dating question only. Nothing of the kind is filmed, referred to on screen, or narrated.

The whole-fruit and cut-fruit distinction is reported by journalism quoting a stallholder and the shrine's lay administrator. It is not established here from any liturgical or scholarly source, and whether it is universal at the site, or a convention of particular stalls, is unverified. The film's opening beat depends on it, so it is checked with the sellers on a pre-visit before anything is shot.

The district. Wikipedia and the OpenStreetMap address both place the town in Monaragala District, Uva Province. At least one travel reference files it under Hambantota District. Monaragala is taken as correct and the variant is recorded because it is the kind of error that propagates.

Press reporting in 2024 alleged organised extortion around the offering stalls at the precinct. This is an unresolved allegation about a real place and named offices, it is not adjudicated here, it is not the film's subject and it is not narrated. It is recorded only because it bears on access and on whether stall material can be filmed without putting anybody at risk.

what_to_film: The offering-stall avenue at night, from the wrist down: betel laid five in a circle with one in the middle, whole fruit stacked into a tower, a garland coiled on top, a second bench where the fruit is being cut. Both kinds of tray in the same frame if they occur that way; never arranged so that they do.

One tray's whole journey as an object: built, paid for, carried, handed across the counter into the dark, waited for, returned lighter. Framed throughout on hands, forearms and the tray, and abandoned the moment a face enters the frame.
Camphor: one tablet lit on a blackened stone and burned to nothing in a single unbroken take, no cut, no cheat.
The oil lamps end-on at long lens so the row of flames compresses into one continuous line, with the crowd thrown completely out of focus behind them.

The crowd only ever as mass and texture: a long lens filling with moving cloth, lamplight and smoke at a density where nobody is resolvable; and the same fixed frame at three or four in the morning with the avenue empty and the bulbs still burning.
The painted curtain at the shrine front, filmed from where any visitor stands, held long enough to become the object it is. Nothing beyond it, ever.
Sand: printed by a night's traffic, swept, and printed again; a raking low-angle at first light before the sweepers start.

The river before sunrise — one static wide, shallow water over sand, old trees, no one in the frame — and the whitewashed stupa to the north in flat light, for the one cold open exterior in a film of enclosed night.
The morning after, in hard flat daylight: the ground, crushed garlands, split coconut shell, bottles, a loader working a heap. The scale of what was carried in, filmed as volume.
suggested_location.access: By road to the town, which sits at the end of the southern dry-zone routes: roughly 20 km north of Tissamaharama, about 228 km from Colombo, on sealed road all the way, with an airstrip at Weerawila for charter. The precinct is entered on foot and barefoot; footwear is left outside and the ground is sand. The precinct is effectively open at all hours because pilgrims arrive through the night, with formal observances morning and evening. Filming is not a single permission: the shrine complex is administered by the devalaya under its Basnayake Nilame, the stupa and its temple by its own chapter, the mosque and mausolea by their own trustees, and the whole town falls within a declared sacred area with its own authority, so any serious shoot needs consent from several bodies and should not assume one covers another. Photography inside active shrine buildings is reported as discouraged and in places prohibited, and the inner apartment is closed to all but the shrine's officiants; the film is designed so that every frame can be obtained from the public ground outside the doorways. Drone is treated as prohibited throughout — a dense sacred precinct, several shrine bodies, and the boundary of a strictly protected national park immediately south. Accommodation is in the town and at Tissamaharama; during the annual fortnight both are full and vehicle movement in the town is restricted.
suggested_location.best_time: Night, through the year, for the body of the film: the hours either side of the evening observance for the lamps and the stalls, and the small hours for the empty version of the same frames. The annual Esala fortnight — which in 2025 ran from a flag-hoisting on 26 June to the water-cutting at the river on 11 July, and which falls in July or early August in most years — for the density and for the volume of offerings, though nothing of the procession is needed as an event. First light at the river for the one open frame. The dry months, because the sand is the film's ground surface and reads completely differently wet, and because the unsealed margins and the river crossing are the first things to go in heavy rain.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 26 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground or against printed editions. Coordinates are the OpenStreetMap node for the Ruhunu Maha Kataragama Devalaya, which returns the address as Pita Veediya, Kataragama, Monaragala District, Uva Province; that is also the district given by Wikipedia, and the one travel reference filing the town under Hambantota is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than silently dropped. The Mahavamsa wording is Geiger's translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, chapter 19, read directly rather than quoted from a secondary page, because the Kajaragama line is the load-bearing fact of the historical thread and the 'no corroboration in the Mahavamsa' judgement depends on knowing what the chronicle does say. The Dutugemunu vow was tested exactly as instructed and it did not survive: it is asserted by the shrine's own site, by the devotee archive and by essentially all the press and travel writing, and the Wikipedia article on the temple states outright that it has no corroboration in the Mahavamsa. No primary or scholarly source stating it was located. It is therefore held in what_is_disputed and the film treats it as a story rather than a date. The Kiri Vehera dating was tested the same way and produced three mutually incompatible attributions plus a fourth variant; they are listed separately and nothing is averaged. The 'regional king Mahasena in the sixth century BC' formula is flagged because it is internally doubtful and is the kind of unsourced repetition this project has been caught by before. The two Obeyesekere papers were confirmed through their publisher and indexing records — Man 12 (1977) 377–396 and Journal of Asian Studies 37:3 (May 1978) 457–476 — and their arguments are taken from abstracts and summaries, not from the full texts, which are paywalled; that limitation matters because the nineteenth-century decline and the post-1930 resurgence are the most consequential claims in the thread. Pathmanathan, Bechert and Younger are cited at second hand through the Wikipedia article on the temple and were not read. The inner sanctum material — no image, painted curtains not drawn, only kapuralas passing, a yantra in a casket, and the sentence 'It is never displayed — nor is its existence either confirmed or denied' — comes from the principal devotee-run archive of the site, which is a partisan source about its own subject; it is consistent with the Wikipedia article and with the temple's own description of its shrines, but no independent scholarly confirmation was obtained. The whole-fruit and cut-fruit distinction on which the film's first beat rests is carried by two independent journalistic sources, one quoting a stallholder and one quoting the shrine's Basnayake Nilame, and by nothing else; it is marked for checking with the sellers before shooting and the film has a drop_if for it. Figures were kept apart rather than reconciled throughout: the annual attendance figure of 'over 500,000' is unsourced travel-page material and is not used; the pada yatra distances and durations vary by a factor of more than two between sources and none is spoken; the counted figures that are used — 31,000 completing the route in 2024, more than 10,000 entering the park on the first day of 2025, and nearly 1,500 tonnes of waste from the 2024 festival — are attributed in what_is_certain to the wildlife authorities and to Mongabay respectively, and the waste figure is marked in what_must_be_real for re-checking with its issuing authority before it is spoken in the film. Access, permissions, whether several administering bodies would each consent, current photography rules and drone rules are all unverified; drone is assumed prohibited. Four Wikimedia Commons files were confirmed to exist through action=query&titles before their URLs were written. Every candidate image was opened and looked at, and images were rejected on the group's floor rather than on quality: the frontal views of the shrine and of the inner gate both contain pilgrims, one of them apparently at the shrine itself, and were dropped even though they are the most illustrative pictures available; the 1819-captioned photograph of the shrine was dropped both because it shows a posed group of identifiable people and because a photograph cannot date from 1819; and several results returned by a search for the site's name are shrines of the same dedication in other districts and were discarded. The four kept images contain no people at all.

unknowns: Whether any of the administering bodies — the devalaya, the stupa's chapter, the mosque's trustees, the sacred area authority — would permit filming at all, and whether a permission from one is recognised by the others. Nothing has been approached.

Whether the whole-fruit and cut-fruit distinction is recognised and described that way by the sellers at this site. Two journalistic sources say so; the film's opening beat depends on it and it is unverified on the ground.
Whether a tray can be filmed across the counter and back without any frame resolving a face, and whether the officiants would agree to hands-only coverage of the handover.
Current photography rules inside and immediately outside the shrine buildings, which are reported inconsistently, and whether tripods or a long lens are treated differently from a phone.
Whether the crowd densities the film assumes actually occur outside the annual fortnight, and whether the empty small-hours version of the same frames exists on ordinary nights.
Drone rules over the sacred area and over the adjoining national park. Assumed prohibited; not confirmed.
The 1,500-tonne waste figure's issuing authority and the basis of the measurement, which are reported at second hand.
Whether the 2024 reporting on extortion around the stalls describes a situation that still obtains, and what it means for filming at the stalls safely and without exposing anybody.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. The historical_thread is desk research by web search only: chronicle wording is from a published translation online, the two scholarly papers are summarised from abstracts rather than read, and the inner-sanctum material comes from a devotee-run archive writing about its own site. No scene or shot is decided here.
